entries.text: The authors propose a single multi-speaker VTS system by transferring learned speech-content representations from voice conversion to a lip-to-index model.
entries.condition: Novelty claim; abstract and introduction.
entries.quote: This paper proposes a novel multi-speaker VTS system based on cross- modal knowledge transfer from voice conversion (VC)

entries.text: VQCPC is claimed to produce discrete phoneme-like acoustic units that encode linguistic content and can serve as Lip2Ind prediction targets.
entries.condition: Units are quantized VC content-encoder outputs; Lip2Ind is trained from corresponding lip sequences.
entries.quote: vector quantization with contrastive predictive coding (VQCPC) is used for the content encoder of VC to derive discrete phoneme-like acoustic units

entries.text: The authors claim that a reference-utterance speaker embedding controls generated speaker identity, while a pitch predictor controls F0 contour.
entries.condition: At use time, the speaker encoder receives a reference utterance and the pitch predictor estimates F0 from video-derived content.
entries.quote: the speaker identity controlled by effective speaker representation s′ 𝑘, which is produced by the speaker encoder from a reference utterance

entries.text: The authors frame the discrete intermediate units as a more interpretable lips-to-speech mapping than prior end-to-end black-box mappings.
entries.condition: Motivation contrasted with the cited multi-speaker VTS approaches [16,17].

entries.text: The abstract claims state-of-the-art quality, naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity under constrained- and open-vocabulary conditions.
entries.condition: The reported comparisons are GRID and LRW, with Lip2Wav and XTS baselines where available; see Table 1 entries below.

entries.text: The stated contributions are VQCPC acoustic-unit derivation, Lip2Ind cross-modal transfer, and a multi-speaker VTS system tested on GRID and LRW.
entries.condition: The LRW claim concerns the paper's benchmark experiments, not unrestricted continuous-vocabulary speech.

entries.text: Each video is described as 25-FPS imagery paired with mel frames at a 10-ms shift (100 FPS); the lip sequence has one frame for every four mel frames.
entries.value: 25 FPS video; 10 ms shift; 100 FPS mel; T/4 lip frames
entries.unit: frames/s; milliseconds; frames/s; relative sequence length
entries.condition: The paper describes K paired videos and aligns image sequence length to T/4 of the speech feature sequence.

entries.text: The VC system has speaker encoder, content encoder, pitch predictor, and decoder; the VQCPC content encoder downsamples mel frames by two.
entries.condition: VC is separately trained on GRID speech and LRW speech; the Lip2Ind network later substitutes its content encoder.
entries.quote: Four modules are contained: speaker en- coder, content encoder, pitch predictor and decoder

entries.text: The VC content encoder uses a codebook with 200 units of 160 dimensions each.
entries.condition: Reported VC implementation setting; no codebook-size ablation is reported.
entries.quote: the VQ-codebook of content encoder has 200 160- dim units

entries.text: The pitch predictor is a two-layer 1-D convolutional network with 384 channels, kernel size 3, ReLU, layer normalization, then a linear 1-D-F0 output.
entries.unit: layers; channels; kernel width; output dimension
entries.condition: Applied in the VC model; paper says F0 is difficult to predict from visual features.

entries.text: The VC decoder is a four-block Conformer with 384-dimensional attention, 2 heads, 1536-dimensional FFN, and 31×1 convolution kernels.
entries.condition: Decoder maps acoustic units, speaker representation, and F0 to mel-spectrograms.

entries.text: GRID has 33 speakers, about 1,000 videos per speaker, 52 words, and constrained indoor recordings.
entries.unit: speakers; videos per speaker; vocabulary words
entries.condition: GRID benchmark; paper describes the recording condition as constrained and indoor.

entries.text: GRID test speakers are s1, s2, s4, and s29; experiments use either all 33 speakers for training or exclude those four, and videos of each speaker are randomly divided 80/10/10.
entries.value: 4 test speakers; 33-speaker or 29-speaker training pool; 80/10/10 train/dev/test
entries.condition: The all-speaker condition intentionally includes training videos from test identities (seen speakers); excluding the four yields the unseen-speaker condition.

entries.text: Speech features are 80-dimensional mel-spectrograms using a 400-point FFT and 10-ms shift; F0 uses the same shift.
entries.condition: Speech feature extraction for GRID and LRW.

entries.text: Dlib facial landmarks are used to crop and resize the lip region to 96×96 pixels.
entries.condition: Image preprocessing for GRID and LRW lip sequences.

entries.text: Separate VC models for GRID and LRW are trained with Adam for 150 epochs, 15 warm-up epochs ramping the learning rate from 1e-6 to 1e-3, and batch size 256.
entries.condition: Two separate dataset-specific VC trainings; the paper does not report random seeds or repeated runs.

entries.text: Lip2Ind uses a 3-D transposed convolution to upsample lips by 2, ResNet-18, a four-layer multiscale temporal CNN with kernel branches 3/5/7, and a softmax index classifier.
entries.unit: factor; architecture depth; layer count; kernel widths
entries.condition: Lip2Ind predicts the VQ-codebook index sequence as an N-way classification problem.
entries.quote: The Lip2Ind network is modiﬁed from [30], and consists of a 3D-transposed convolutional network

entries.text: Lip2Ind is trained with Adam for 80 epochs, cosine scheduling from 3e-4, weight decay 1e-4, batch size 32, random 88×88 crops, horizontal flips, and mixup.
entries.value: 80 epochs; LR 3e-4; weight decay 1e-4; batch 32; crop 88×88
entries.unit: epochs; learning rate; weight decay; examples/batch; pixels
entries.condition: Training uses the described data augmentations; seed and augmentation probabilities are not reported.

entries.text: Mel-spectrograms are converted to waveform using Griffin-Lim or a Parallel WaveGAN vocoder trained on LibriTTS.
entries.condition: VCVTS rows report GL and PWG separately; baselines use GL according to their cited papers.
entries.quote: mel-spectrograms are converted to waveform by using Grifﬁn-Lim (GL) [33] or Parallel WaveGAN (PWG) [34] vocoder that is trained on LibriTTS

entries.text: The comparison uses multi-speaker Lip2Wav and XTS; both use GL, and XTS is only implemented on GRID because its training requires unavailable LRW speaker labels.
entries.condition: XTS is absent from LRW results; Lip2Wav is the only baseline in LRW Table 1.
entries.quote: both of which use GL following their papers

entries.text: Objective evaluation reports PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, MCD, and F0-RMSE; no objective-metric confidence intervals are tabulated.
entries.condition: Table 1 evaluates GRID seen/unseen speakers and LRW unseen speakers; MCD and F0-RMSE units are not specified in the paper.

entries.text: Twenty subjects provide 5-point MOS ratings (1 bad to 5 excellent) for speech naturalness and speaker similarity; 60 generated utterances are randomly selected, with 15 per each of four GRID test speakers explicitly stated.
entries.value: 20 subjects; 5-point scale; 60 utterances; 15 per GRID test speaker
entries.condition: Paper says the 60-utterance sampling is for both GRID and LRW but only gives the 15×4 allocation for GRID; LRW allocation is unclear.
entries.quote: 20 subjects are recruited to give 5-point MOS

entries.text: Figure 2 illustrates unit sequences for four GRID speakers saying “red” (R EH1 D); a shared index occurring at least twice within the same phoneme is highlighted.
entries.condition: Qualitative visualization only; it is not a phoneme-alignment accuracy evaluation.

entries.text: Figure 3 visualizes speaker embeddings with t-SNE from reference and generated utterances; lip sequences are randomly chosen from test speakers.
entries.condition: Reference utterances include speakers seen or unseen during training; this is a qualitative visualization, not a separate metric test.

entries.text: On GRID, all systems perform better for seen than unseen test speakers, which the authors interpret as susceptibility to out-of-domain speakers.
entries.condition: GRID test speakers s1, s2, s4, s29; seen versus excluded-from-training conditions; see Table 1 scores.

entries.text: The authors say VCVTS with GL gives the best GRID PESQ, STOI, ESTOI, and F0-RMSE for seen and unseen speakers; MCD is not included in that superiority sentence.
entries.condition: GRID Table 1; GL VCVTS versus XTS/Lip2Wav GL and PWG VCVTS.

entries.text: The authors report that VCVTS with GL or PWG beats Lip2Wav on LRW, an unconstrained, larger-vocabulary benchmark.
entries.condition: LRW Table 1, unseen speakers; only Lip2Wav and VCVTS rows are reported.

entries.text: The authors say PWG is worse than VCVTS+GL on GRID objective metrics except MCD, attributing artifacts to the neural vocoder.
entries.condition: GRID objective Table 1 comparison of the two VCVTS vocoders.

entries.text: For subjective MOS, the authors report that VCVTS scores above Lip2Wav and XTS on naturalness and speaker similarity, and PWG above GL.
entries.condition: GRID and LRW subjective evaluations; Table 1; XTS results exist only for GRID.

entries.text: The authors interpret t-SNE clusters of each reference utterance with its generated utterances as evidence that speaker embeddings capture speaker characteristics.
entries.condition: Qualitative visualization using the VCVTS speaker encoder; no cluster-separation score is reported.
entries.quote: each reference utterance and its corresponding generated utterances can form a distinct clus- ter

entries.text: The authors concede that VTS performance degrades substantially for unseen GRID speakers and attribute this to the limited number of GRID training speakers.
entries.condition: Reported especially as degraded speaker similarity; comparison is seen versus unseen test identities.
entries.quote: the limited number of speakers of GRID for training a VTS system that generalizes poorly to out-of- domain speakers

entries.text: The authors concede that PWG can introduce acoustic artifacts that reduce objective scores even though it sounds more realistic in subjective ratings.
entries.condition: PWG versus GL vocoder comparison; objective and subjective outcomes differ.

entries.text: The authors identify cross-domain and multilingual VTS as future work rather than demonstrated capabilities.
entries.condition: Scope limitation in conclusion.

entries.text: The reported SOTA claim is bounded by the two baselines and benchmark conditions actually compared; XTS is not included for LRW.
entries.condition: GRID compares XTS and Lip2Wav; LRW compares Lip2Wav only.

entries.text: No random seeds, number of independent training runs, or repeated-evaluation protocol is reported for VC, Lip2Ind, or the Table 1 results.
entries.condition: Applies to GRID/LRW training and objective/subjective evaluations; results are presented as single values and MOS intervals only.

entries.text: A dev split is named, but checkpoint selection, early stopping, hyperparameter selection, and whether the final or best checkpoint is evaluated are not stated.
entries.condition: GRID uses a stated train/dev/test split; LRW uses default train/dev/test splits.

entries.text: Exact objective-test utterance counts and the precise evaluation-sample selection procedure are not given; the approximate corpus sizes and split ratios do not determine exact test counts.
entries.condition: GRID and LRW objective evaluations; MOS sampling is described separately and incompletely for LRW.

entries.text: No session-level split or recording-session overlap check is described; GRID partitioning is by random videos within speaker.
entries.condition: Potential session dependence cannot be assessed from the reported split protocol.

entries.text: LRW speaker disjointness is an assumption rather than a verified condition because speaker labels are unavailable; actual cross-split speaker overlap is not reported.
entries.condition: The authors use default LRW splits and assume speakers in different splits are exclusive.
entries.quote: assume that speak- ers in different splits are exclusive considering that the speaker la- bel of each video is unavailable

entries.text: For the Table 1 runs, the source, duration, and split membership of reference utterances for speaker conditioning, and their overlap with training/evaluation audio, are not specified.
entries.condition: The system uses reference-utterance speaker representations; the paper does not fully operationalize reference selection for the main evaluation.
entries.quote: which is produced by the speaker encoder from a reference utterance

entries.text: The MOS protocol does not report the LRW utterance allocation, rater assignment, blinding, presentation randomization, repetitions per rater, or the method used to compute 95% confidence intervals.
entries.condition: The paper reports 20 subjects, a 5-point scale, and 60 selected utterances, but gives only the 15-per-speaker GRID allocation.

entries.text: Units/scaling for MCD and F0-RMSE and any normalization of the objective scores are not specified; Table 1 reports metric values without units.
entries.condition: Table 1 objective metrics; do not interpret F0-RMSE values as a stated Hz quantity.

entries.text: No chance-level result, random baseline, or metric-specific null reference is reported.
entries.condition: Objective and subjective evaluations in Table 1.

entries.text: The paper does not specify normalization of the paper's mel features or lip-image pixels, beyond their dimensions, FFT, and crop size.
entries.condition: Speech and image inputs for GRID/LRW; distinguish from the Resemblyzer dependency's preprocessing documented in its repository.

entries.text: No language model, lexicon, transcript-based decoding aid, or LM decoding condition is described; the paper reports acoustic-unit prediction followed by vocoding.
entries.condition: Applies to the reported VTS decoding pipeline and comparisons.

entries.text: The paper links the Resemblyzer dependency, but does not identify a VCVTS source-code repository, revision, or experiment scripts; the linked repository is not the VCVTS training/evaluation implementation.
entries.condition: Repository checked: Resemblyzer README and available package/demo scripts; no paper-specific VCVTS training or evaluation scripts are supplied there.

entries.text: The linked Resemblyzer implementation defaults to its bundled pretrained.pt checkpoint unless a custom weights path is supplied; the paper does not identify checkpoint or repository revision, so the exact used weights are not established.
entries.condition: Dependency-code default only; do not treat this as proof of the exact checkpoint used in the paper.
entries.quote: the speaker encoder is taken from Resemblyzer2 and outputs a 256-dim vector

entries.text: The linked Resemblyzer audio preprocessing resamples to 16 kHz, normalizes volume to -30 dBFS in increase-only mode, and trims long silences with VAD; the paper omits these encoder-input details.
entries.value: 16 kHz; -30 dBFS; increase-only volume normalization; VAD silence trimming
entries.condition: Condition in linked dependency code, not verified as the authors' exact experiment configuration.

entries.text: The linked Resemblyzer encoder uses a 3-layer LSTM with 256 hidden dimensions, applies ReLU, and L2-normalizes the output; these model details are not stated by the paper.
entries.condition: Dependency implementation; the paper reports a 256-dimensional speaker vector but not the architecture or normalization.

entries.text: The linked Resemblyzer encoder uses 40-channel mel features with 25-ms windows and 10-ms hops for its speaker embedding input; the paper does not state these encoder-specific feature settings.
entries.value: 40 mel channels; 25 ms window; 10 ms hop
entries.condition: Dependency code setting; distinct from the paper's reported 80-dimensional mel features for VC training.

entries.text: Video content is encoded by an aligned 3D-convolution/ResNet/LSTM visual front end, but that stream also carries speaker cues; the intended split assigns linguistic content to visual features and identity to the auxiliary embedding.
entries.condition: Video-to-speech with aligned video and audio; no explicit text representation.

entries.text: Speaker information is concatenated with post-LSTM visual features before the Tacotron2 audio decoder. SI uses a learned discrete-speaker vector; SE uses an utterance-level embedding from a frozen Xie et al. speaker-recognition network, projected 512→32; SE-norm standardizes the embedding because its original small scale can cause the model to ignore it.
entries.condition: Speaker-conditioned synthesis; SI is identity-based, while SE/SE-norm condition on an audio-derived speaker embedding.
entries.quote: we concatenate the speaker identity to the visual features (obtained after the LSTM) and the augmented vector is then passed to the audio decoder.

entries.text: A speaker classifier is trained on visual features; either adversarial entropy maximization or gradient reversal encourages the visual representation to lose speaker identity while preserving audio reconstruction.
entries.condition: Classifier variants are linear or MLP, operating on temporally pooled visual features.

entries.text: The GRID corpus has 34,000 video-audio samples from 34 speakers and a 52-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: WER is measured using a Kaldi time-delay neural-network ASR trained on TED-LIUM 2 with a finite-state-grammar language model derived from GRID word sequences; synthesis uses reduced Mel spectrograms, SSRN, and Griffin-Lim. No random seed is stated.

entries.text: The seen-speaker setup tests four speakers, with 900 training, 50 validation, and 50 test samples per speaker.
entries.condition: Seen GRID speakers; 52-word vocabulary. No random seed is stated.

entries.text: For unseen-speaker evaluation, videos from unseen speakers are paired with target voice identities from seen speakers; content is scored by WER and identity control by EER, using cosine distances between speaker embeddings. The random pairings preclude reference-based MCD, STOI, and PESQ.
entries.condition: Unseen video speakers / seen target identities; EER uses synthesized-natural embedding pairs and a cosine-distance threshold. WER uses the GRID-derived finite-state-grammar ASR setup. No random seed is stated.
entries.quote: pair videos of unseen speakers with target voice identities of seen speakers.

entries.text: The discrete-ID SI model gives the best speaker-control results on average but can synthesize only voices seen during training; SE and SE-norm support embedding-based target voices. The paper notes a control–intelligibility trade-off.
entries.condition: Unseen video speakers paired with seen target identities; Table II compares WER and EER.

entries.text: The SE variant with frame dropping and a dispel/linear classifier reports WER 35.5 and EER 12.7 on the unseen-video/seen-target evaluation.
entries.condition: Table II, SE group row 12; unseen video speakers paired with seen target identities.

entries.text: FastLTS conditions a non-autoregressive acoustic decoder on visual features from the video; the decoder maps them to acoustic features, with visual features duplicated to match acoustic-sequence length.
entries.condition: Lip-to-speech from silent video; no LM, random seed, or multiple-output sampling condition stated.

entries.text: Generation is parallel and the acoustic features feed a GAN-based HiFi-GAN waveform generator; no explicit latent-variable or sampling mechanism for multiple candidates is described.
entries.condition: Inference; mel-spectrogram output is auxiliary training supervision and is not fed to the waveform generator; no LM or seed stated.

entries.text: The reported setup does not establish a jointly trained multi-speaker decoder; extending the model to multi-speaker settings is listed as future work.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav experiments include three speakers from the dataset; speaker-ID conditioning and multi-speaker decoding details are not stated.

entries.text: FastLTS mel-spectrogram inference speedup over Lip2Wav at 3-second input length.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav test comparison, Chemistry Lectures speaker; 3-second input; batch size 1 on Intel Xeon E5-2678 CPU and NVIDIA RTX-2080Ti GPU; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: FastLTS waveform synthesis speedup over Lip2Wav at 3-second input length.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav test comparison, Chemistry Lectures speaker; 3-second input; batch size 1 on Intel Xeon E5-2678 CPU and NVIDIA RTX-2080Ti GPU; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: FastLTS MOS for Chess Analysis: Quality 3.79±0.09, Intelligibility 3.82±0.10, Naturalness 3.59±0.08.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav dataset test split (same split as prior work [24]); Chess Analysis, one of three tested speakers, vocabulary over 5,000 words; Amazon Mechanical Turk, over 300 respondents per item; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: FastLTS MOS for Chemistry Lectures: Quality 3.84±0.10, Intelligibility 3.73±0.11, Naturalness 3.87±0.09.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav dataset test split (same split as prior work [24]); Chemistry Lectures, one of three tested speakers, vocabulary over 5,000 words; Amazon Mechanical Turk, over 300 respondents per item; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.condition: Lip2Wav dataset test split (same split as prior work [24]); Hardware Security, one of three tested speakers, vocabulary over 5,000 words; Amazon Mechanical Turk, over 300 respondents per item; no LM or seeds stated.

entries.text: The primary representation of speaking style is implicit and speaker-specific: the paper studies individual styles in a single-speaker setting and does not specify a separate style embedding.
entries.condition: Primary unconstrained setting; per-speaker data are about 20 hours with a 5K+ word vocabulary; 90/5/5 train/validation/unseen-test split by different videos; no seed reported.

entries.text: The multi-speaker variant conditions on a provided speaker embedding, but is only a word-level LRW baseline; the paper does not describe generating multiple voice alternatives from the same lip sequence.
entries.condition: LRW test split; random identities; single words in short phrases; WER obtained using Google ASR API; seed not stated.
entries.quote: feed a speaker embedding as input to our model.

entries.text: An attention-based Tacotron 2 sequence-to-sequence decoder conditions speech steps on prior speech and encoded face features, and autoregressively generates mel-spectrogram frames with L1 reconstruction loss.
entries.condition: Lip2Wav training/inference; 3-second visual training windows; autoregressive decoding; no beam, sampling, or seed settings stated.

entries.text: The speech target is an 80-bin mel spectrogram computed from 16 kHz audio with an 800-sample window and 200-sample hop.
entries.condition: Speech representation used for Lip2Wav training; no seed variation reported.

entries.text: The final waveform is reconstructed from predicted mel spectrograms with Griffin-Lim; neural vocoders were avoided because their performance was poor on the model's less accurate mel outputs.
entries.condition: At test time, consecutive T-second windows are decoded independently and concatenated with a small overlap; no vocoder seed reported.

entries.text: Homophene ambiguity is addressed with an implicit speech-level language model from sequence context and decaying teacher forcing, rather than an explicit multi-voice output mechanism.
entries.condition: Single-speaker task; teacher forcing used through about 30K iterations, then gradually decayed; no multiple-hypothesis decoding or random seeds reported.

entries.text: No ASR word error rate or any recognition-based intelligibility test of the synthesized speech is reported; intelligibility rests on STOI and ESTOI, although both cited baselines [16,17] report WER in their own papers.
entries.condition: Checked: Abstract, Secs. 1-4, Table 1, Fig. 1-3 captions; no WER, ASR or transcript-based metric.
entries.quote: Following previous works [16, 17], we adopt three standard speech quality metrics

questions.q: What exactly supports the state-of-the-art claim, and how broad is the comparison?
questions.answer: The authors report better objective and MOS results than Lip2Wav and XTS where tested, but XTS is GRID-only and LRW compares only against Lip2Wav; the claim is bounded by those baselines and the two datasets.

questions.q: Are the reported test speakers truly held out from training?
questions.answer: GRID includes both seen test identities (the all-speaker training condition) and unseen identities (the four named test speakers excluded from training). LRW speaker disjointness is assumed because speaker labels are unavailable, not verified.

questions.q: How reproducible and statistically stable are the reported comparisons?
questions.answer: The paper gives model and optimizer settings but no seeds, independent-run counts, checkpoint-selection procedure, exact objective-test counts, or objective-score uncertainty. MOS intervals are reported, but the interval method and several listening-test controls are absent.

questions.q: What conditions control speaker identity at inference, and what remains unspecified?
questions.answer: A speaker encoder embeds a reference utterance, while a pitch predictor supplies F0. The main evaluation does not specify reference-audio provenance, duration, selection, or overlap; dependency code documents preprocessing and embedding normalization but does not establish the exact paper checkpoint.

questions.q: What are the authors' clearest conceded limitations?
questions.answer: Performance drops for unseen GRID speakers, PWG can harm objective metrics through artifacts, and cross-domain and multilingual conditions remain future work.

questions.q: (writer to reader, Mira et al. 2104.13332) GRID unseen split, ASR used and its WER on real audio, unseen GRID and LRW rows, seeds?
questions.answer: 50/20/30 speaker-disjoint split of all 33 GRID speakers; pre-trained GRID ASR, 4.23% WER on real audio; unseen GRID PESQ 1.47, STOI 0.523, WER 23.13% (Table VII); LRW 500 words WER 42.51% (Table IX); no seeds or repeated runs.
